 1                  I.     INTRODUCTION AND QUALIFICATIONS

 2   Q1.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A.    My name is Victor Martinez, and my business address is 100 N. Stanton Street,

 4         El Paso, Texas 79901.

 5

 6   Q2.   HOW ARE YOU EMPLOYED?

 7   A.    I am employed by El Paso Electric Company ("EPE" or "Company") as the Director

 8         of Energy Resources.

 9

10   Q3.   HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY SUBMITTED TESTIMONY IN THIS CASE?

11   A.    Yes. I submitted Direct Testimony on August 6, 2026, in support of EPE’s

12         Amended Application for Revision of its Retail Electric Rates.

13

14   Q4.   ARE YOU SPONSORING ANY EXHIBITS IN THIS FILING?

15   A.    No.

16

17                   II.   PURPOSE OF REBUTTAL TESTIMONY

18   Q5.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

19   A.    My rebuttal testimony has two purposes. First, I respond to and correct operational

20         assumptions made by City of Las Cruces witness Ted Thomas underlying his Direct

21         Testimony on the Santa Teresa 150 MW solar PV/150 MW battery energy storage


                                                1
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      VICTOR MARTINEZ

 1         system (“BESS”) facility (“Santa Teresa Project”). Specifically, I address Mr.

 2         Thomas’s erroneous assumptions regarding EPE’s operation of the Santa Teresa

 3         Project including charging and operating the BESS above the 50 MW approved for

 4         New Mexico, round-trip efficiency losses, the project’s 150 MW interconnection,

 5         and the purpose for which the Santa Teresa Project and the Carne 130 MW solar

 6         PV/65 MW BESS (“Carne Project”) were procured. Second, I provide an update

 7         regarding the commercial-operation status of the Santa Teresa Project in response to

 8         the direct testimonies of New Mexico Public Regulation Commission Advocacy

 9         Staff (“Staff”) witnesses Orland Whitney and Jonah Mauldin.

10

11   Q6.   HOW DOES YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY RELATE TO THE

12         STIPULATION THAT EPE JOINED IN THIS CASE?

13   A.    My rebuttal testimony responds to the direct testimonies of Staff and intervenor

14         witnesses in this case as noted above. EPE is a Stipulating Party to the

15         Comprehensive Stipulation and fully supports its approval. If the Commission

16         approves the Stipulation, the individual issues I address in my rebuttal testimony

17         need not be separately addressed.

18

19                III.    SANTA TERESA PROJECT OPERATIONS

20   Q7.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF THIS SECTION OF YOUR REBUTTAL

21         TESTIMONY?


                                                2
                                   EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                   REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                       VICTOR MARTINEZ

 1   A.    The purpose of this section of my rebuttal testimony is to correct the erroneous

 2         operational assumptions underlying City of Las Cruces witness Ted Thomas’s

 3         Direct testimony on the Santa Teresa Project.

 4

 5   Q8.   WHAT ARE MR. THOMAS’ OPERATIONAL CONCERNS?

 6   A.    Mr. Thomas questions whether EPE’s operation of the Santa Teresa Project,

 7         including the use of the Santa Teresa solar facility to charge the 150 MW BESS,

 8         results in another jurisdiction receiving a portion of the renewable energy paid for

 9         by New Mexico customers. Mr. Thomas also raises concerns regarding operation

10         of the BESS capacity above the 50 MW approved for New Mexico, associated

11         round-trip efficiency losses, and the effect of the Santa Teresa Project’s 150 MW

12         interconnection on the usefulness of the BESS. As demonstrated below, each of

13         these concerns derives from Mr. Thomas’s misunderstanding of how EPE operates

14         the Santa Teresa Project to serve New Mexico.

15

16   Q9.   FOR CONTEXT, CAN YOU PROVIDE A HIGH-LEVEL EXPLANATION

17         OF HOW EPE CHARGES AND DISPATCHES THE 150 MW SANTA

18         TERESA BESS?

19   A.    EPE’s Energy Resources department operates EPE’s available resources on an

20         integrated-system basis. EPE does not dispatch any resource on a jurisdictional basis.

21         Typically, solar energy from the integrated resource is diverted to the battery during


                                                  3
                                    EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                    REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                        VICTOR MARTINEZ

 1          periods of high solar generation and relatively low customer load, and is dispatched

 2          from the BESS when solar production has declined and customer demand remains

 3          relatively high. Charging and discharging decisions are based on system conditions,

 4          customer load, available generation, reliability requirements, resource limitations,

 5          and economic conditions.

 6

 7   Q10.   DO NEW MEXICO CUSTOMERS LOSE CREDIT FOR SOLAR ENERGY

 8          THAT IS DIVERTED TO CHARGE THE SANTA TERESA BESS?

 9   A.     No. New Mexico receives the renewable energy credits (“RECs”) for Santa Teresa

10          Project solar energy invoiced under the purchased power agreement (“PPA”)

11          regardless of whether that solar energy is delivered directly to the point of

12          interconnection or delivered to the BESS for charging. Accordingly, the operational

13          decision to direct Santa Teresa solar energy to the BESS rather than to immediately

14          deliver that energy to the grid has no impact on RECs or any credit for the renewable

15          energy produced by the Santa Teresa solar facility. This treatment is consistent with

16          Commission approval of the project’s entire solar energy output as a Renewable

17          Energy Act (“REA”) procurement for purposes of meeting EPE’s renewable

18          portfolio standard requirements with the provision of safe, reliable service. EPE

19          witness Enedina Soto discusses how that energy is reflected in EPE’s jurisdictional

20          allocation factors in her direct and rebuttal testimony.

21



                                                   4
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      VICTOR MARTINEZ

 1   Q11. DOES EPE’S ENERGY RESOURCES DEPARTMENT LIMIT OPERATION

 2        AND USE OF THE SANTA TERESA BESS TO THE 50 MW APPROVED

 3        FOR NEW MEXICO REA PURPOSES?

 4   A.   No. The regulatory treatment of the project does not impact or limit physical

 5        operations. As stated above, Energy Resources operates EPE’s available resources

 6        on an integrated-system basis.      EPE does not dispatch any resource on a

 7        jurisdictional basis. The available BESS resource is operated based on system

 8        conditions, customer load, available generation, reliability requirements, resource

 9        limitations, and economic conditions.

10

11   Q12. WHY      WOULD       EPE     USE    AVAILABLE         SANTA      TERESA       BESS

12        CAPABILITY ABOVE THE 50 MW APPROVED AS A NEW MEXICO REA

13        PROCUREMENT?

14   A.   EPE must continuously balance generation and load across its system. During

15        periods of high solar generation and relatively low customer load, the amount of

16        Santa Teresa solar energy credited to New Mexico may exceed New Mexico’s load

17        during that hour. Charging available BESS capacity allows EPE to store energy that

18        is not needed at that time and make that energy available later in the day when solar

19        production has declined and customer demand remains relatively high.

20                From an operational perspective, using available BESS capability above 50

21        MW can therefore benefit New Mexico customers by increasing EPE’s ability to


                                                  5
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      VICTOR MARTINEZ

 1        shift solar energy from periods when the energy exceeds contemporaneous load

 2        requirements to periods when that energy has greater operational value. It can also

 3        reduce the need to curtail renewable generation or make additional off-system sales

 4        solely to balance generation and load.

 5                Accordingly, using available Santa Teresa BESS capability above the 50

 6        MW approved for New Mexico does not, by itself, disadvantage New Mexico

 7        customers. Rather, greater use of the available BESS provides additional flexibility

 8        to preserve and shift solar energy for use during periods when that energy is more

 9        valuable to the system and its customers.

10

11   Q13. MR. THOMAS EXPRESSES CONCERN THAT USING BESS CAPACITY

12        ABOVE THE 50 MW APPROVED FOR NEW MEXICO COULD IMPAIR

13        NEW MEXICO CUSTOMERS BECAUSE OF ROUND-TRIP EFFICIENCY

14        LOSSES. DO YOU AGREE?

15   A.   No. While storing energy in a battery involves round-trip efficiency losses, those

16        losses must be considered along with the benefits of the storage to New Mexico

17        customers, including the consequences if there is not sufficient BESS capacity

18        available to store the solar energy.

19                During     periods   when      Santa   Teresa   solar   production   exceeds

20        contemporaneous load requirements, limiting BESS charging to 50 MW could

21        reduce EPE’s ability to store that excess solar energy. Depending on system


                                                   6
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      VICTOR MARTINEZ

 1        conditions, the remaining energy may need to be sold off-system or, if it cannot

 2        otherwise be accommodated, curtailed. Curtailment would also reduce the amount

 3        of renewable energy available to serve New Mexico customers.

 4                 The relatively small amount of energy that is lost through the battery’s

 5        round-trip efficiency must be weighed against the ability to preserve a substantially

 6        greater amount of solar energy for later use. From an operational perspective, I

 7        would not consider the round-trip efficiency loss, standing alone, a disadvantage to

 8        New Mexico customers. Using available BESS capacity above 50 MW can allow

 9        EPE to retain more of the available Santa Teresa solar energy for later use rather

10        than risk losing the opportunity to use that energy for EPE customers altogether.

11

12   Q14. ONCE ENERGY HAS BEEN STORED IN THE SANTA TERESA BESS,

13        DOES ENERGY RESOURCES DISPATCH THE SUBSEQUENT BESS

14        DISCHARGE ACCORDING TO THE JURISDICTION OR SOURCE

15        ASSOCIATED WITH THE CHARGING ENERGY?

16   A.   No. As I discussed above, EPE operates its available resources on an integrated-

17        system basis. Once the BESS is available for discharge, Energy Resources operates

18        it as part of EPE’s integrated resource portfolio. The decision to discharge the BESS

19        is based on system needs, customer load, available generation, reliability

20        requirements, resource limitations, and economic conditions.

21                This operational treatment should not be confused with the separate


                                                7
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      VICTOR MARTINEZ

 1        regulatory or accounting treatment used to assign costs, energy, or other benefits

 2        among jurisdictions.

 3

 4   Q15. MR. THOMAS ALSO RAISES CONCERNS REGARDING THE 150 MW

 5        INTERCONNECTION LIMIT FOR THE SANTA TERESA PROJECT AND

 6        THE RESULTING USEFULNESS OR REAL-WORLD CAPACITY OF THE

 7        BESS. DOES THE 150 MW INTERCONNECTION PREVENT EPE FROM

 8        UTILIZING THE FULL OUTPUT CAPABILITY OF THE BESS?

 9   A.   No. The fact that the Santa Teresa solar facility and BESS share a 150 MW

10        interconnection does not mean that the BESS is limited to some lesser amount of

11        output at all times. The amount of interconnection capability available to the BESS

12        depends in part on the simultaneous output of the solar facility.

13                Solar production and BESS discharge do not necessarily reach their

14        maximum levels at the same time. Energy Resources can charge the BESS while

15        solar generation is available and discharge the BESS after solar generation declines.

16        When solar generation is zero, such as during evening periods after sunset, the full

17        150 MW interconnection capability can be available for BESS discharge, subject to

18        the BESS’s availability and other applicable operating limitations. Therefore, the

19        150 MW interconnection does not prevent the BESS from providing its full 150 MW

20        output capability during those periods.

21



                                                 8
                                   EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                   REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                       VICTOR MARTINEZ

 1   Q16. MR.    THOMAS’S         DIRECT     TESTIMONY        SUGGESTS        THAT      EPE

 2        PROCURED THE SANTA TERESA PROJECT AND THE CARNE

 3        PROJECT TO MEET ANTICIPATED LARGE-LOAD GROWTH. DO YOU

 4        AGREE?

 5   A.   No. The Santa Teresa Project and Carne Project were each procured from

 6        competitive solicitations and subsequently approved by the Commission under the

 7        Renewable Energy Act as part of a renewable energy act procurement plan to meet

 8        EPE’s obligations under the Renewable Energy Act as well as short- and long-term

 9        capacity needs, unrelated to projected large-load growth. The Carne Project was

10        selected through a competitive procurement process in 2022 and subsequently

11        approved by the Commission under the Renewable Energy Act as a REA Plan

12        procurement in its REA Plan filing for 2023. The Santa Teresa Project was selected

13        through a competitive procurement process in 2024 and subsequently approved by

14        the Commission under the Renewable Energy Act as a REA Plan procurement in its

15        REA Plan filing for 2026. The subsequent emergence of additional large-load

16        requirements may affect EPE’s current and future resource-planning needs, but it is

17        unrelated to the purpose and timing of EPE’s procurement of the Carne Project and

18        Santa Teresa Project.

19

20   Q17. DOES YOUR TESTIMONY MEAN THAT FUTURE LARGE-LOAD

21        GROWTH CANNOT CREATE ADDITIONAL RESOURCE NEEDS FOR


                                               9
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      VICTOR MARTINEZ

 1        EPE?

 2   A.   No. Large-load growth can affect EPE’s future load forecasts and resource

 3        requirements. My testimony is limited to clarifying that the Carne and Santa Teresa

 4        projects were not procured because of Project Nucleus or the subsequently identified

 5        large-load requirements. The RFP purposes and procurement chronology

 6        demonstrate that they were not.

 7

 8               IV.   UPDATE ON COMMERCIAL OPERATION OF

 9                                 SANTA TERESA PROJECT

10   Q18. STAFF WITNESSES WHITNEY AND MAULDIN CONDITION SUPPORT

11        FOR INCLUDING SANTA TERESA BESS CAPACITY COSTS IN BASE

12        RATES ON THE FACILITY BEING IN SERVICE BEFORE THOSE RATES

13        TAKE EFFECT. CAN YOU PROVIDE A STATUS UPDATE ON THE

14        SANTA TERESA PROJECT?

15   A.   Yes. The Santa Teresa Project achieved full commercial operation on October 12,

16        2026, and is now available for operation as part of EPE’s resource portfolio.

17

18   Q19. HOW DOES THIS SUBSEQUENT DEVELOPMENT AFFECT THE

19        CONCERNS IDENTIFIED IN STAFF’S DIRECT TESTIMONY?

20   A.   Mr. Whitney’s testimony accurately reflected the information available in the record

21        when his testimony was prepared. However, the factual status of the project has since


                                                10
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                     VICTOR MARTINEZ

 1        changed. The Santa Teresa Project achieved full commercial operation on October

 2        12, 2026.

 3                This also satisfies the condition identified by Mr. Mauldin. The Santa

 4        Teresa Project achieved commercial operation before the rates established in this

 5        case will become effective. Accordingly, the commercial-operation condition

 6        identified in Mr. Mauldin’s testimony has been satisfied.

 7

 8                                 V.    CONCLUSION

 9   Q20. PLEASE SUMMARIZE THE CONCLUSIONS OF YOUR REBUTTAL

10        TESTIMONY.

11   A.   My rebuttal testimony establishes two principal points.      First, the operational

12        assumptions underlying Mr. Thomas’s concerns regarding the Santa Teresa Project

13        do not accurately reflect how Energy Resources operates those resources. New

14        Mexico receives credit for Santa Teresa solar energy invoiced under the PPA

15        whether that solar energy is delivered directly to the point of interconnection or

16        delivered to the BESS for charging. The 50 MW of BESS capacity approved for

17        New Mexico is a regulatory allocation and does not represent a physical operating

18        limitation on the Santa Teresa BESS. Energy Resources operates the available BESS

19        as part of EPE’s integrated resource portfolio based on system conditions, customer

20        load, available generation, reliability requirements, resource limitations, and

21        economic conditions. Similarly, round-trip efficiency losses do not by themselves


                                               11
                                  EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                  REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      VICTOR MARTINEZ

 1        establish that New Mexico customers are harmed by use of available BESS capacity,

 2        and the shared 150 MW interconnection does not prevent the BESS from providing

 3        its full output capability when sufficient interconnection capability is available.

 4        Finally, the Carne and Santa Teresa projects were not procured in response to Project

 5        Nucleus or subsequently identified large-load service requirements. Subsequent

 6        large-load growth may affect EPE’s current and future resource needs, but it did not

 7        cause these original procurements.

 8                Second, the Santa Teresa Project has now achieved full commercial

 9        operation on October 12, 2026, satisfying the commercial-operation condition

10        identified by Mr. Mauldin for including the applicable Santa Teresa BESS capacity

11        costs in Base Rates.

12

13   Q21. DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

14   A.   Yes, it does.
